subtitle: Prepare a navigator with the right information, run a meeting where everyone has a clear role, handle disagreement with respect and close the loop afterward.
audience: For assessors, case managers, county and tribal partners and other staff who meet people alongside a cultural navigator. It builds on What a Cultural Navigator Does and does not change data practices rules, program rules or who makes decisions.

lessons.title: Before the meeting: consent and a good briefing
objectives: Explain why the person's written informed consent comes before sharing private information with a navigator.
Share the minimum a navigator needs for the meeting ahead, not the whole file.
Agree on roles with the navigator before the person arrives.
Prepare a short briefing that a navigator can use to help the person take part.
lessons.teaching:
A good meeting with a navigator starts days before it, with the person's agreement. In Minnesota, a government entity can release private data about a person to someone else when that person gives informed consent. The Department of Administration's Data Practices Office explains that informed consent is written permission, and that valid consent must be voluntary, explain why the release is needed and say what the known consequences are. Use your program's release form and follow its rules. A navigator from a community organization is outside the agency, even when everyone trusts them.

Once the person agrees, share what the navigator needs for the meeting ahead, and no more. Usually that is the purpose of the meeting, what decisions might come up, any deadlines, which interpreter is booked and what the person has said they want help with. The navigator rarely needs a full case history, and the person may not want them to have it.

Agree on roles before the meeting starts. Who explains the program? Who interprets? Who helps the person follow along and ask questions? Who makes or records the decision? Five minutes on a phone call can prevent the most common problem in these meetings, which is two people trying to do the same job, or nobody doing one.

A useful briefing is short and plain. It tells the navigator what the meeting is for, what might be hard to understand and what the person needs to leave knowing. The navigator brings what you cannot: how this process is likely to land for this family, and what questions they may be too uncomfortable to ask.
lessons.keyPoint: Get the person's written consent, share only what the meeting needs and agree on roles before anyone sits down.
lessons.example: Practice case: The case manager has a planning meeting next week. The person has asked for a navigator from a community organization to come. The navigator calls and asks the case manager to send over everything in the file so they can be fully prepared.
lessons.question: What should the case manager do?
choices: Send the full file, since the person asked for the navigator.
Decline to share anything, since the navigator is not agency staff.
Check that the person has signed a release, then share what the meeting needs and talk through roles with the navigator.
feedback: Asking for a navigator is not the same as agreeing to share everything. The person decides what is shared, and the meeting rarely needs the whole file.
This protects data, but it leaves the navigator unprepared and the person without the help they asked for. A signed release lets you share what is needed.
This respects the person's choice, gives the navigator what they need to help and prevents the role confusion that derails these meetings.
lessons.reflection: When you prepare for a meeting, what do you assume the other people already know? What would a navigator need to hear from you?
lessons.action: Before your next meeting with a navigator, write a three-line briefing: what the meeting is for, what might be hard to understand and what the person needs to leave knowing.

check.question: Under Minnesota's data practices guidance, what is informed consent to release private data?
check.correct: Written permission from the person, given voluntarily, that explains why the release is needed and its known consequences.
wrong: A spoken yes at the start of the meeting.
The person's choice to bring a navigator to the meeting.
check.feedback: The Data Practices Office describes informed consent as written permission that is voluntary and explains why the release is needed and its consequences. Bringing a navigator is a choice about support, not consent to share data.

lessons.title: Running a three-way meeting
objectives: Speak to the person, not to the navigator or the interpreter.
Pace a meeting so the person can follow, ask questions and decide.
Check understanding by asking the person to say what happens next in their own words.
Notice when a navigator starts answering for the person, and bring the conversation back to them.
lessons.teaching:
A meeting with a person, a navigator and a staff member is really a meeting for the person. Face them and speak to them, even when an interpreter is carrying your words or the navigator knows the answer. If you turn to the navigator to ask about the person, you teach everyone in the room that the person is not the one who decides.

Slow down. Explain one step at a time and stop after each one. Leave silence for questions, because many people will not interrupt someone from an agency. A navigator can help here by asking the questions the person may not ask: What happens if we say no? How long will this take? Who do we call?

Check understanding without testing anyone. A simple way is to ask the person to tell you, in their own words, what happens next and what they need to do. If the answer is not what you expected, the gap is in the explanation, not the person. Try again in plainer words, or ask the navigator whether another way of explaining might help.

Sometimes a navigator, trying to help, starts answering for the person. Gently bring the conversation back. You might say, "Thank you, that helps me understand. I'd like to hear from you too," and ask the person directly. A good navigator welcomes this, because their job is to help the person speak, not to speak for them.
lessons.keyPoint: Speak to the person, go one step at a time and check understanding by asking what happens next. The navigator helps the person speak; they do not speak for them.
lessons.example: Practice case: During a meeting, the assessor asks the person about their daily routine. Before the person can answer, the navigator explains the routine in detail. The person nods along and says nothing.
lessons.question: What should the assessor do?
choices: Thank the navigator, then ask the person directly to describe their day in their own words.
Thank the navigator and record their answer, since it was detailed.
Ask the navigator to stay quiet for the rest of the meeting.
feedback: This values the navigator's help and returns the conversation to the person, who is the one whose life and services are being discussed.
The detail may be accurate, but the answer needs to come from the person. Nodding is not the same as agreeing.
This may embarrass the navigator and the person, and it loses the help the person asked for. A gentle redirect usually works.
lessons.reflection: In meetings, who do you tend to look at when you ask a question? What would change if you looked at the person every time?
lessons.action: At the end of your next meeting, ask the person to tell you in their own words what happens next. Note anything you would explain differently.

check.question: Which is the best way to check that a person understood the next steps?
check.correct: Ask them to say in their own words what happens next and what they need to do.
wrong: Ask, "Do you have any questions?" and move on if they say no.
Ask the navigator whether the person understood.
check.feedback: Many people say they have no questions even when they are unsure. Hearing the next steps in the person's own words shows what landed and what needs another try.

lessons.title: When you and the navigator disagree
objectives: Recognize that a navigator may advocate for the person in ways that create tension with staff.
Raise a disagreement with a navigator respectfully, and privately first when possible.
Separate what the rules require from what is habit or convenience.
Keep the person's choice at the center when staff and navigator see things differently.
lessons.teaching:
Navigators and staff will sometimes disagree, and that is a sign the role is working. The National Center for Cultural Competence quotes Jezewski and Sotnik's description of a cultural broker as "a go-between, one who advocates on behalf of another individual or group." Advocacy means the navigator will sometimes push. They may say a provider list leaves out options that fit the family, or that a deadline is unfair given what the family is dealing with.

Start by asking what the navigator is seeing. Often they know something you do not, about the family or about how a step lands in their community. Then be honest about what you can and cannot change. Separate what a law or program rule requires from what is simply how your team usually does things. Habits can often bend. Rules usually cannot, but there may be an exception process, a supervisor who can decide or a different path to the same goal.

Raise disagreements privately first when you can. Arguing in front of a family can frighten them or make them feel they have caused trouble. If the disagreement is about the family's own choices, though, the family belongs in the conversation, because the choice is theirs, not yours or the navigator's.

When you cannot resolve it, say so plainly and name the next step: who decides, how the person can appeal or ask for review and when you will follow up. A disagreement handled with respect often builds more trust than an easy meeting.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask what the navigator is seeing, separate rules from habits and keep the person's choice at the center. Disagree privately first when you can.
lessons.example: Practice case: After a meeting, the navigator tells the case manager that the family was only offered providers who do not speak their language. The case manager believes there are no other providers nearby. The supervisor joins the conversation.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor suggest?
choices: Tell the navigator the list is the list, and move on.
Ask the navigator which providers they know of, check whether any could serve the family and tell the family what was found.
Agree to change providers right away, before checking anything.
feedback: This ends the disagreement but may keep a real option from the family. The navigator may know providers your list does not.
This takes the concern seriously, checks it against what is actually possible and brings the result back to the family, who make the choice.
This responds quickly, but a change made before checking may not be possible and could disrupt services that are working.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time someone pushed back on how you do your work. What helped you hear it, and what made it harder?
lessons.action: List two things in your process that are habits rather than rules. Next time a navigator questions one of them, start by asking what they are seeing.

check.question: A navigator and a case manager disagree about a family's service choice. Whose decision is it?
check.correct: The family's, with clear information from both about the options and the rules.
wrong: The case manager's, because they are responsible for the plan.
The navigator's, because they know the family's culture.
check.feedback: Staff hold the rules and the plan, and the navigator helps the family understand and speak. The choice among available options belongs to the person and their family.

lessons.title: Closing the loop and keeping the partnership
objectives: Tell the navigator what happened next, with the person's agreement.
Send written follow-up in plain language that the person and navigator can both use.
Treat a navigator's time as real work that deserves credit and planning.
Build a working agreement with the organizations that provide navigation.
lessons.teaching:
The meeting is not the end of the work. After it, the person needs a clear note of what was decided, what happens next and who to call. Write it in plain language, and when the person needs another language, use your program's translation process. With the person's agreement, send the navigator what they need to follow up, such as dates and contacts.

Close the loop with the navigator too. If a service was approved, a provider called or a step fell through, the navigator often hears about it from the family first. When they are kept informed, they can explain what is happening instead of guessing. When they are left out, they lose standing with the family, and the family may lose trust in both of you.

A navigator's time is real work. Navigators often work for community organizations with small budgets and big caseloads. Plan meetings around their schedule as well as yours, give notice when something changes and credit their help when you describe how a case was resolved. M Health Fairview's cultural brokers, for example, spend much of their time based at trusted community organizations. That kind of partnership works best when both sides know what to expect.

Where your program works with navigators often, a short written agreement with the partner organization helps. It can cover how referrals happen, how consent is handled, how to reach each other and how you will talk about problems. The agreement keeps the partnership from depending on one good relationship between two people.
lessons.keyPoint: After the meeting, give the person a plain-language note of what happens next, keep the navigator informed with consent and treat the partnership as real, planned work.
lessons.example: Practice case: Three weeks after a meeting, the navigator calls the newer colleague. The family has heard nothing and is worried their request was denied. In fact, it was approved a week ago, and the letter is still being processed.
lessons.question: What should the newer colleague do?
choices: Tell the navigator the letter will arrive soon and end the call.
Call the family directly and ask them why they contacted the navigator instead of the office.
Confirm the family has agreed to updates being shared, tell the navigator the request was approved and what happens next, and ask the program manager about telling families sooner.
feedback: This is accurate but leaves the navigator and the family without the reassurance and detail they need, and it misses the pattern.
People often go first to someone they trust. Questioning that choice can damage trust in the office.
This gives the family good news through someone they trust, within their consent, and raises the gap so the next family does not wait in silence.
lessons.reflection: After a meeting, who in your work is most likely to be left wondering what happened? How could one short message change that?
lessons.action: After your next meeting with a navigator, send a short plain-language summary of what was decided and what happens next, to the person and, with their agreement, to the navigator.

check.question: Why does keeping a navigator informed after a meeting matter?
check.correct: The family often asks the navigator first, and an informed navigator can explain what is happening instead of guessing.
wrong: So the navigator can make the next decision about services.
Because navigators must approve every step in the plan.
check.feedback: Navigators do not decide or approve services. They help families understand what is happening, which they can only do when they are kept informed, with the person's agreement.

cards.back: Written, voluntary permission from the person to release their private data, explaining why the release is needed and its known consequences.
What the meeting is for, what might be hard to understand and what the person needs to leave knowing.
Before the meeting: who explains, who interprets, who supports the person and who decides.
Ask the person to say in their own words what happens next. A gap means the explanation needs another try.
Separate what a law or rule requires from how your team usually does things. Habits can often bend.
A plain-language note to the person, and an update to the navigator with the person's agreement.

aid.heading: Before the meeting
items: Confirm the person's written release, using your program's form.
Share only what the meeting needs.
Book a qualified interpreter if one is needed.
Agree on roles: who explains, interprets, supports and decides.
Send the navigator a three-line briefing.

aid.heading: During the meeting
items: Face and speak to the person.
Go one step at a time and leave room for questions.
If the navigator answers for the person, thank them and ask the person directly.
Ask the person to say what happens next in their own words.

aid.heading: When you disagree
items: Ask what the navigator is seeing.
Talk privately first, unless the choice is the family's to make.
Name who decides and how to ask for review.

aid.heading: After the meeting
items: Send a plain-language note of what happens next.
Update the navigator with the person's agreement.
Raise any delay or confusing step with your supervisor or program manager.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Administration, Data Practices Office — Informed Consent
sources.note: Describes informed consent under Minnesota Statutes, section 13.05, subdivision 4, as written permission to release private data, and lists what valid consent requires under Minnesota Rules 1205.1400: voluntary, in writing, explaining why the release is needed and its known consequences.

sources.note: Describes cultural brokers assisting with team meetings, attending appointments and court with families, and encouraging families to work with case managers.
